description: Team AreA 51 is building health monitoring software for astronauts on long space missions. We bring coding, web development and AI/machine learning, plus a love of education and storytelling. We're friendly and open to new ideas, whether it's your first hackathon or your fifth. We're looking for people with coding, web dev or AI skills, plus anyone into pollution, waste and resources, or storytelling. We speak English, Russian and Turkish. Join us and help keep astronauts healthy!
summary:
AreA 51 – Astronaut Health Monitoring System
AreA 51 is an interactive health-monitoring platform designed to help astronauts assess their physical and mental well-being during long-duration space missions.
Our solution combines three key functions: SEE, CHECK, and ACT. SEE visualizes six health and mission-safety indicators, including heart rate, oxygen saturation, hydration, body temperature, suit pressure, and radiation exposure. CHECK allows astronauts to record daily sleep, mood, blood pressure, and blood glucose, generating a personalized wellness score. ACT identifies abnormal readings, explains potential health risks, provides actionable recommendations, and indicates when medical assistance is necessary.
The platform also features interactive 3D visualization, color-coded alerts, and health-trend tracking to make complex information easier to understand.
By addressing NASA's five major spaceflight hazards, AreA 51 helps astronauts recognize warning signs, monitor changes over time, and make informed decisions when immediate medical support from Earth is unavailable.
Our goal is to make astronaut health monitoring more accessible, understandable, and proactive, supporting safer and more independent space exploration.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

AreA 51 is an astronaut health-monitoring dashboard built around self-assessment. It has three parts:

1. SEE – Six vitals update every second, each colour-coded green / amber / red against defined safe ranges:

heart rate (with a moving ECG line), blood oxygen (SpO2), hydration, body temperature, suit pressure and cumulative radiation dose. A one-sentence summary at the top says whether every indicator is inside its safe range.

2. CHECK – A daily check-in for sleep, mood, blood pressure and blood glucose. Each answer gets its own status, and the answers combine into one wellness score.

3. ACT – When a value leaves its safe range:

- a red alert banner shows the value and the limit it crossed;

- a guidance panel explains what the metric is, why it matters, which spaceflight hazard causes it (radiation, isolation/confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, hostile closed environment) and what to do now, including when to contact the flight surgeon;

- the event is saved with a timestamp and shown on the mission timeline chart.

More features:

- Clickable 3D suit/body inspector (Three.js) that shows suit-zone readings: visor, glove, boot and coolant temperature, O2 tank, battery.

- EVA map with distance, ETA and rover range.

- Spaceflight hazard explainer that links each vital to the hazard behind it.

- A live data card with the latest NASA space-weather notifications and linked astronaut health studies.

- Status badge for every data feed: live, cached or offline snapshot. The badge switches to "Signal lost" when telemetry stops.

HOW IT WORKS

- Frontend: React 19 + TypeScript, built with Vite and styled with Tailwind CSS. Three.js loads only when the 3D inspector opens.

- Environment data: live requests to NASA and NOAA APIs (see NASA Data). Every response is cached in localStorage and falls back to the last real snapshot, so the app keeps working with no network. That matters on a spacecraft with delayed or broken contact with Earth.

- Crew vitals: no live astronaut telemetry is public, so vitals come from a physiological model. Each metric is a mean-reverting bounded random walk with slow drift, clamped to realistic ranges. Heart rate rises during EVA, hydration drains and refills, and radiation dose only goes up. Every 30–90 seconds an anomaly is eased in for testing, or you can trigger one by pressing "A".

- Real hardware ready: a WebSocket data source takes one JSON telemetry message per sample, so real wearables or suit sensors can replace the simulator without changing the UI.

- All thresholds are in one config file, and all guidance text is in another, so flight surgeons could tune them without touching the code.

- Responsive: under 1024 px it is a full-screen mobile app; on desktop it shows a phone frame next to a timeline chart and the 3D inspector. First load is about 85 kB gzipped JS.

BENEFITS

- Built for autonomy: the crew sees not only that something is wrong but why and what to do, without waiting 40 minutes for a round trip to Earth.

- Plain language instead of raw numbers, for crew members who are not doctors.

- Works offline thanks to cached real data.

- Open, configurable and ready for real sensors.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

We want to show that a clear self-assessment tool can make astronauts their own first line of medical care on Artemis surface stays and Mars transit. The same design (live status plus plain-language advice that works offline) also fits people on Earth who cannot reach a clinic: Caspian offshore oil and gas crews (a problem we know first-hand in Azerbaijan), polar stations, submarines and remote mountain villages.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Three.js, lucide-react icons, Archivo and IBM Plex Mono fonts, WebSocket API, browser localStorage, NASA Open APIs (api.nasa.gov), NOAA SWPC JSON services, NASA OSDR Biological Data API.

AI ASSISTANCE

Parts of the source code were written with an AI coding assistant (Claude Code), under our team's design and review. The idea, the feature choices and the use of the data are our own.
